items.output: Snow fell softly all night blanketing the cabin in white. Inside a fire crackled casting warm light on wooden walls. We played board games and shared hot cocoa with stiff fingers. Outside we tracked deer through fresh powder then skied slow circles in the clearing. At dusk we watched the stars appear one by one above the pines. The world felt still and gentle and kind.

The snow fell steadily through the morning, muffled and quiet, blanketing the pines until even their dark green boughs looked soft, almost invisible beneath the white. Inside the log cabin, the wood stove crackled, casting flickering shadows across the worn pine walls. A teakettle sang on the hearth, steam rising like a silent promise of warmth. Below, the creek—usually a chattering companion—flowed thick and silvery beneath the ice, its song turned to a hushed hum. Snow draped the roof in deep folds, and the world beyond the frosted windows existed only as a blur of white and evergreen. Later, we walked out, boots crunching, breath curling in the air like ghosts, returning with rosy cheeks and fingers stiff with cold, eager for cocoa and the quiet thrill of being untethered, suspended in winter’s hush. The first time I submerged my face in the pool, water rushed in and made me gasp, but I held on to the edge, determined to try again. My instructor’s calm voice guided each stroke, helping me coordinate movements that initially seemed impossible. Each lesson made me realize how much my fear had held me back, not my ability. Slowly, my arms and legs found rhythm, transforming awkward splashes into smooth glides across the water.Breathing became deliberate, and soon I was making progress without gripping the wall. By the end of summer, I swam laps with steady breaths and a quiet pride that no one could take away.
